full_judgment:
3. The plaintiff-opposite parties filed the above mentioned suit praying for a decree for declaration of title and partition on the averments stating, inter alia, that the disputed land measuring 15 decimal of land situated under Shibganj Upazila of Mouza Nayala Bhanga appertaining to SA Khatian No. 672 RS Khatian No. 1492, Hal Dag No. 1948 and SA 2886 was recorded in the name of 4 sons of Wahedullah Mondal, namely, Seraj Mondal, Reaz Mondal, Foring Mondal and Afimuddin Mondal. During the time they used to cultivate the suit land jointly. Sirajuddin Mondal died leaving behind his wife Jarimon Bibi and 4 sons namely. Shakaruddin, Jafar, Rabu Mondal alias Bhutta Mondal and Paku and 2 daughters namely, Negar Nessa and Khatimon Nessa as his heirs. In the SA record other properties were recorded in Khatian No. 672 measuring 1.09 acres of land. The wife of Sirajuddin Mondal and sons Shakaruddin, Jafar and Paku sold their share measuring 2½ decimals in the year 1972 by a Kabala being No. 8609 to opposite party No.1 and became disinterested. Rabu Mondal and daughter Khatomon Nessa, the plaintiff-opposite party Nos. 3-4 and other daughter Negar Nessa being dead her heirs were plaintiffs-opposite party Nos. 5-10. Foring Mondal died leaving behind his widow Alekjan Bibi, daughters Funni Bibi and sons Saber Ali. Subsequently the said Saber Ali transferred 1½ decimal of land of his shares to plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 by a deed of ewaj, being No. 8593 in the year 1992. Alekjan Bibi widow of Foring Mondal and daughter Funni Bibi, sold 1-1/4 decimal of land to Shamsuddin defendant-petitioner No. 21 and his brother by a registered deed No. 6469. 

 9. The learned Counsel Mr Md Bazlul Kabir, appearing on behalf of the defendant-respondent-petitioner, submits that the learned Subordinate Judge, Nawabganj was absolutely wrong and erroneous in allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial Court, the appellate Court did not discuss the evidence on record and came to a wrong and fallacious finding which is liable to be set aside. Next, he submits that the appellate Court without applying his judicial mind and without proper assessment of the evidence on record, particularly the Salishmana which was produced by the defendant before the trial Court as well as before the appellate Court, which was not a all considered by the learned Subordinate Judge, Nawabganj and acted illegally in reversing the judgment and decree passed by the learned Munsif, Shibganj. On the other hand, the learned trial Court after discussing the evidence on record and the facts and circumstances of the case and also on considering the very old documents i.e. Salishnama and the Salishnama, which was executed by the predecessor of the plaintiff-appellant-opposite parties and put their signature in the Salishnama and also considering the genuineness of Salishnama and considering the genuineness of possession of the defendant for 60 years and the record of right of RS Khatian dismissed the suit of the plaintiff which was absolutely right and justified. The learned Counsel further submits that in reversing the judgment of the trial Court the appellate Court is required to reverse the material finding of the trial Court with reference to the evidence on record. But the learned Subordinate Judge, Nawabganj, without referring to the evidence on record and without consideration of Salishnama, observed that since the Salishnama was not exhibited before the trial Court it has not been proved and hence it cannot be considered. The learned Counsel further submits that since the Salishnama was produced before the Court, the appellate Court ought to have considered that Salishnama should be taken into judicial notice though not exhibited due to laches of the lawyers. In this connection be referred sections 56-57 of the Evidence Act and emphatically submits that the appellate Court committed error in not considering the Salishnama so long it was produced before the Court, the appellate Court should take it into judicial notice and ought to have considered the genuineness of the Salishnama, as such, the appellate Court failed to observe the legal obligation under sections 56-57 of the Evidence Act wherein it has been clearly stated: 

 12. On a meticulous examination of the evidence on record, papers, documents, RS Khatian and the judgment of the Courts below and other connected papers, it transpires that the trial Court discussed the evidence and also perused the relevant papers and documents and considered the material evidence on record particularly, Salishnama produced by the defendant and made his clear observation. The lower appellate Court without applying his judicial mind and without discussing the evidence on record and without proper assessment of the evidence gave much importance on the question that the Salishnama which was not proved and exhibited it cannot be considered but the learned Subordinate Judge, Nawabganj ought to have considered the facts and circumstances of the case as well as section 56 of the Evidence Act wherein it has been laid down that fact judicially noticeable need not be proved and no fact of which the Court will take judicial notice need be proved. The learned Subordinate Judge, Nawabganj ought to have discussed and considered the material facts of the case that the defendant has been in possession of the suit land more than 60 years ago without any disturbance and the RS Khatian also prepared in the name of the defendant which creates a claim of right of adverse possession.  15. The impugned judgment of the trial Court transpires that in arriving in its finding the said Court carefully considered the material facts and circumstances of the case and also the material evidence on record, the legal position and the act of possession and also the RS Khatian and Salishnama. The learned trial Court did not commit any error of law and illegality in arriving at its finding because the plaintiff could not be able to prove his possession in the suit land by adducing oral evidence. The lower appellate Court committed an error of law and came to a wrong finding occasioning failure of justice in not considering the prolonged possession of the defendant over the suit land.
